title: In secret
hookLine: let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth (Matthew 6:1–4)
tomorrow: why does the heart follow the treasure, and not the other way?

cards: Night, in a small town. A father with three daughters and no money for their marriages, and their future hanging on it. Something comes through the window and lands on the floor with a thump: a bag of gold.
Tradition says it happens again, another night. The third time, the father is waiting. He runs out after the stranger and catches him.
It's Nicholas, a young neighbor, who tradition says will one day be bishop of Myra. And Nicholas asks him for one thing: don't tell anyone.

teach.b: That's the old story of Saint Nicholas, told in the Golden Legend, and some readers hear in it a root of the gifts children find from a giver they never see.
The story reads like a few lines from the Sermon on the Mount, acted out.

teach.h: NOT TO BE SEEN OF THEM.
teach.b: "Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them."

And then: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly." So, light or secret? Read the two side by side.
Salt and light says let them see your good works, so they glorify your Father. This says don't give to be seen of them. The difference is the aim.

teach.h: LIGHT SHOWS THE WORK; SECRET HIDES YOU.
teach.b: Light shows the good work and sends the praise past you.
Secret hides the giver, so the praise can't land on you at all.
Same sermon, same target: not you. That's the teaching Christians carry from it: almsgiving, giving to the poor, is a hidden practice, done for God and not for an audience.
In the Catholic calendar, this passage is read on Ash Wednesday, at the start of Lent, the season of prayer, fasting and almsgiving.

how: Christians practice almsgiving, often quietly, alongside prayer and fasting; Catholics hear Matthew 6:1–6 and 16–18 on Ash Wednesday, at the start of Lent. Saint Nicholas's feast is December 6, and some families mark it with small gifts left in shoes.

keeping your beliefs hidden from your family

games.q: you paid for the order of the person behind you in the drive-through. the cashier asks if she should tell them who it was. what does 'in secret' say?
o: no, just tell them someone wanted them to have it.
yes, so they know who to thank and can pay it back.
yes; the sermon says let people see your good works.
games.why: the left hand doesn't know: the gift lands, and the giver stays out of it.

practice: Take a slip of paper and write one kind, true line for someone you'll see this week: a coworker, a neighbor, the person at the front desk. Don't sign it.
Fold it, decide where you'll leave it, and then sit with the gift already given and nobody to thank you.

wordCard.voice: In secret: giving so quietly that even your other hand doesn't know, seen only by the Father which seeth in secret.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 6:4: in secret, in the hidden place.

carryVoice: Keep this close: the left hand doesn't know, and the gift still lands. Light or secret, the praise goes past you.
